# Agents, Frameworks, and Sandboxes {#sec-agents-practice}

An agent is a software system that repeatedly asks a model what to do,
interprets the proposal, decides whether the proposal is allowed, performs any
approved effect, records the result, and decides whether to continue. The model
is one component inside that system; scheduling, authorization, durable
storage, and the security boundary belong to the code around it.

The ReAct work introduced a widely used pattern for interleaving model reasoning
with actions in an external environment [@yao2023react]. That pattern explains
how a trajectory, the sequence of reasoning steps, actions, and observations in
one run, can be generated. A production runtime must add the controls that the
prompting method does not provide: typed actions, complete mediation (a check on
every action at the point where it executes), bounded execution, durable state,
recovery, approval, isolation, and evidence.

The practical unit is therefore an **agent release**, the counterpart of the
adaptation release in @sec-training-practice: an agent execution contract, a
versioned controller, a reviewed tool catalog, an isolation policy, an
evaluation report, and a reversible deployment. @sec-agent-architectures
develops the behavioral patterns; @sec-the-harness develops the durable runtime.
This chapter connects them to tool protocols and sandbox enforcement.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-agent-control-loop
//| fig-cap: "A production agent loop. Trusted runtime code validates and authorizes each model proposal, executes allowed actions, records the observation, and decides whether the run may continue."
digraph agent_loop {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, margin="0.12,0.08", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  state [label="Durable state\ncontract • budget • history"];
  context [label="Bounded context"];
  propose [label="Model proposal\nanswer or action"];
  gate [label="Validate + authorize\nallow • deny • approve"];
  execute [label="Execute through broker"];
  record [label="Record observation\nreceipt • usage • checkpoint"];
  stop [label="Terminal state\nsuccess • failure\ncancellation"];

  state -> context -> propose -> gate;
  gate -> execute [label="allowed"];
  execute -> record;
  record -> context [label="continue"];
  gate -> stop [label="denied /\nstop"];
  record -> stop [label="complete /\nbudget"];
}
```

## Freeze the agent execution contract

Framework selection comes after the **agent execution contract**. The contract
states what one run may accomplish, which external effects are permitted, what
evidence proves success, and how the system stops safely. Without it, a demo
that reaches a plausible answer can be mistaken for a dependable application.

| Contract field | Evidence to record |
|---|---|
| Task boundary | Accepted requests, excluded uses, supported environments, and the unit of work |
| Success evidence | Final answer checks, external end-state checks, required artifacts, and uncertainty handling |
| Permitted effects | Read, create, update, delete, communicate, spend, deploy, or execute, each with resource limits |
| Authority | User or workload principal, tenant, delegated actor, allowed tools, scopes, and expiry |
| Data boundary | Inputs the model and tools may read, data that may leave, retention, and redaction |
| Budget | Step, token, cost, wall-clock, concurrency, storage, and network ceilings |
| Human control | Actions requiring preview, approval, dual control, or prohibition |
| Termination | Success, refusal, cancellation, timeout, budget exhaustion, repeated failure, and no-progress rules |
| Recovery | Checkpoint boundary, retry policy, idempotency, compensation, and resume target |
| Rollback | Last-known-good controller, tool catalog, policy, sandbox image, and deployment route |

“Resolve customer issues” names a goal and leaves the boundary open. A usable
contract identifies the system of record, the set of customers, the allowed read
and write actions, the fields that may be disclosed, the evidence that a case is
closed, and the conditions that require escalation. It also distinguishes a draft from an
effect. Composing a refund request and issuing the refund are different
capabilities.

The contract is versioned with the complete served system: model revision,
prompt and context builder, tool schemas, policy, controller, memory rules,
sandbox image, and decoder settings. A change to any of them can change the
trajectory even when the framework package stays fixed.

## Make the control loop explicit

The trusted controller turns a stochastic model proposal into a policy-checked
state transition. One compact formulation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_t &\sim \pi_{\theta}(\mathord{\cdot}\mid C(s_t)), \\
a_t &= V(u_t), \\
d_t &= A(p_t,a_t,r_t), \\
o_t &=
  \begin{cases}
    X(a_t), & d_t=\mathrm{allow}, \\
    \bot, & d_t\in\{\mathrm{deny},\mathrm{approve}\},
  \end{cases} \\
s_{t+1} &= \delta(s_t,a_t,d_t,o_t).
\end{aligned}
$$

where:

- $t$ is the step index, and $s_t$ is the current durable run state;
- $C$ is the context projection that selects and serializes the bounded view of
  state sent to the model;
- $\pi_{\theta}$ is the model distribution with parameters $\theta$, and
  $u_t$ is one sampled model proposal;
- $V$ is schema validation and normalization, and $a_t$ is the validated
  proposed action or final answer;
- $A$ is the external authorization function, $p_t$ is the verified principal
  and policy context, $r_t$ is the current resource snapshot, and $d_t$ is the
  authorization decision `allow`, `deny`, or `approve`;
- $X$ is the credentialed tool executor, $o_t$ is the tool observation, and
  $\bot$ means that no tool was executed; and
- $\delta$ is the deterministic transition function that appends the recorded
  event and produces the next durable state $s_{t+1}$.

The stochastic part ends at the proposal. Schema validation can reject malformed
arguments, but it cannot decide whether a syntactically valid transfer is
authorized. The policy decision uses verified identity and current resource
state outside the model. Human approval is a separate decision when policy
requires it. Tool execution occurs only after authorization, and the observation
is recorded as untrusted data rather than silently promoted to an instruction.

### Keep distinct kinds of state distinct

“Memory” is too vague for recovery design. An agent run usually contains at
least five kinds of state:

| State class | Typical contents | Required treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Conversation history | User messages, model messages, and tool results | Bounded context projection; redaction; not the source of external truth |
| Working state | Plan, selected records, intermediate artifacts, and open questions | Typed schema; versioned updates; may be compacted only with declared loss |
| Durable execution state | Current node, attempts, timers, waits, leases, and cancellation | Persisted before resumption; compatible with controller upgrades |
| External state | Database rows, tickets, payments, deployments, and files outside the run | Re-read before mutation; stable identity; effect receipt or compensation |
| Long-term memory | Cross-run preferences, facts, and summaries | Separate provenance, authorization, retention, and deletion policy |

A message session, a workflow checkpoint, and a trace are separate objects. A
checkpoint records control state and says nothing about whether an external side
effect happened; a trace serves as a replay log only if it records every input
the replay needs. Treating these objects as one “memory” produces duplicate writes,
stale approvals, and recovery that begins from the wrong world state.

### Stop for declared reasons

Every run has a step budget, token budget, cost budget, and wall-clock
deadline. It also stops after a declared consecutive failure
limit or a **no-progress** detector, such as repeated identical actions or no
change in the task state. Tool calls have their own deadline and output limit.

Terminal reasons are part of the API: `succeeded`, `failed`, `refused`,
`cancelled`, `timed_out`, `budget_exhausted`, and `needs_human`. A run that
timed out, was canceled, or ended with its budget exhausted is reported under
that reason and is not counted as a model failure. A run in a terminal state
cannot resume execution under the same identity; a retry creates a linked
attempt with a new lease and an explicit recovery decision.

## Choose control semantics before a framework

Framework names overlap in capability and change faster than the underlying
control patterns. The first choice is therefore the pattern that makes the
required transitions visible; a candidate library is then tested for whether it
implements those semantics.

| Control pattern | Useful when | Main design obligation |
|---|---|---|
| Linear loop | One controller selects a tool or finishes, with little branching | Bound the loop and make every effect pass the same gate |
| State graph | Branches, cycles, joins, waits, and escalation must be explicit | Version nodes and edges; define state migrations and join semantics |
| Durable workflow | Work survives long waits, worker loss, callbacks, and retries | Separate deterministic control from external activities and duplicate-safe effects |
| Filesystem harness | The task is editing, testing, browsing a repository, or operating a CLI | Govern workspace, commands, processes, network, artifacts, and context compaction |
| Supervisor and worker | Independent subtasks can run concurrently under one owner | Give each worker a typed envelope, narrower authority, budget, and return contract |

A handoff transfers responsibility for the next interaction. A bounded subagent
call does not: the parent remains responsible and receives a result. Fan-out and
join require a rule for partial failure, cancellation, ordering, and conflicting
answers. “Multi-agent” does not supply those semantics by itself.

Candidates are compared with a **capability matrix**, one question per runtime
capability, instead of a product leaderboard:

| Capability | Question for the candidate runtime |
|---|---|
| Topology | Are linear flow, cycles, fan-out, joins, and handoffs explicit or hidden in host code? |
| State | What is authoritative, when is it committed, and what are the checkpoint semantics? |
| Recovery | How do retry, resume, cancellation, timeout, and in-flight work behave after a crash? |
| Concurrency | Which updates may race, how are conflicts resolved, and can descendants be canceled? |
| Approval | Can execution pause with an exact proposed effect and resume only after fresh authorization? |
| Tool boundary | Are schemas, policy hooks, idempotency keys, result validation, and error classes available? |
| Provider portability | Which model and tool features actually work across providers, transports, and revisions? |
| Evidence | Can traces, event history, policy decisions, effect receipts, usage, and terminal reasons be exported? |
| Evolution | Can a pending run survive controller, schema, and state migrations? |
| Operations | What must the team host, patch, back up, meter, and support? |

Current libraries expose different combinations of these features. LangGraph
documents checkpointed graph state and interrupts; Pydantic AI delegates durable
execution to workflow integrations; the OpenAI Agents SDK documents both
manager-style orchestration and handoffs [@langgraph2026persistence;
@pydantic2026durable; @openai2026orchestration]. Those facts are inputs to a
local test, and which library fits depends on that test.

The same proof workflow runs against each candidate: two reads, one
approval-gated write, a fan-out and join, and a final state check. The test
crashes the worker after the external write succeeds but before its response is
stored, delivers the same callback twice, cancels an in-flight tool, and
upgrades the controller while approval is pending before resuming. It measures
duplicate effects, lost work, state divergence, latency, cost, and operational
effort. That evidence stays valid longer than a feature table.

## Make recovery safe for effects

Durable execution preserves control state and leaves effects on an external
system without an exactly-once guarantee. A worker can complete a write and fail before
recording the reply, so the controller may see an ambiguous outcome. Many task
queues also provide **at-least-once** delivery, which means a handler may receive
the same logical request more than once.

Every logical side effect therefore has:

- a stable **idempotency key** derived from the run and logical action, not the
  network attempt;
- an intent record written before dispatch;
- an **effect receipt** containing the external operation identity, observed
  resource version, outcome, and time;
- a reconciliation operation that can query an ambiguous result; and
- compensation or escalation when the external API cannot deduplicate safely.

Retries preserve the idempotency key. A retry policy distinguishes transport
failure, retryable tool failure, business rejection, policy denial, and unknown
outcome. An at-most-once attempt avoids automatic repetition but may lose work;
an at-least-once attempt needs duplicate handling. Neither label proves exactly
one real-world effect. Durable workflow documentation makes the same distinction
between replayable control and external activities [@temporal2026workflows;
@aws2026idempotency].

Resume, replay, and reevaluation answer different questions:

- **Resume** continues a pending run from a durable boundary.
- **Workflow replay** rebuilds control state from recorded events without
  repeating recorded effects.
- **Recorded-output test replay** feeds saved model and tool outputs through new
  deterministic controller code.
- **Live reevaluation** calls the model and tools again and may produce a
  different trajectory.

Pending runs carry an explicit version. If a controller or tool contract changes, the
runtime either migrates the saved state, continues with the pinned old version,
or terminates safely. It must not reinterpret an old approval or effect receipt
under new semantics.

### Delegate with a typed envelope

A child agent receives a subset of the parent's authority. The delegation
envelope, the typed record that states what the child may do and must return,
contains:

```yaml
delegation:
  parent_run_id: run_85a
  child_run_id: run_85a_research_2
  objective: "Compare the two named incident records"
  input_refs: [incident_104, incident_119]
  permitted_tools: [read_incident, search_runbook]
  authority_scope: {tenant: acme, access: read_only}
  budget: {steps: 12, tokens: 18000, wall_clock: 5m}
  deadline: 2026-08-07T18:30:00Z
  result_schema: incident_comparison_v2
  completion: "return evidence for every difference"
  return_owner: run_85a
```

The parent validates the result and remains accountable for any later effect.
The child cannot widen its tool set, extend its deadline, or delegate broader
authority than it received. Cancellation propagates down the ownership tree;
results arriving after cancellation are recorded but cannot trigger a new
effect.

## Treat every tool as an effect contract

Beyond a tool name and JSON Schema, the controller needs to know what the tool
reads or changes, what authority it needs, how it fails, and whether it is safe
to repeat.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-agent-tool-boundary
//| fig-cap: "The tool execution boundary. Model output and tool output are both untrusted data; trusted code validates shape, policy, approval, credentials, and receipts around the effect."
digraph tool_boundary {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  proposal [label="Model proposal\nuntrusted"];
  validate [label="Schema validation\nnormalize • reject unknowns"];
  policy [label="Policy decision\nsubject • action • resource"];
  approval [label="Exact-effect approval\nwhen required"];
  executor [label="Credentialed executor\nidempotency • timeout"];
  system [label="External system"];
  result [label="Validate result\nreceipt • taint • provenance"];

  proposal -> validate -> policy -> approval -> executor -> system -> result;
}
```

A versioned tool contract includes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Identity | Namespace, tool version, implementation or package digest, and owner |
| Input schema | Strict types, bounds, enums, required fields, and rejection of unexpected properties |
| Output schema | Typed result, effect receipt, provenance, redaction, and maximum size |
| Preconditions | Required resource state, caller identity, tenant, and policy version |
| Postcondition | Observable state that proves success rather than a reassuring message |
| Side-effect class | Read-only, reversible write, irreversible write, communication, spend, or code execution |
| Idempotency | Business key, duplicate behavior, reconciliation, and compensation |
| Runtime | Timeout, cancellation, retry classes, rate and concurrency limit, and error taxonomy |
| Data and authority | Data classification, allowed destinations, credential scope, and approval rule |

The executor validates arguments again at the execution boundary. It checks the
principal, tenant, resource, current version, and policy even if the controller
already checked them. This is complete mediation and least privilege in the
sense described by Saltzer and Schroeder [@saltzer1975protection]. A tool server
must not trust a model-provided resource handle as proof of ownership.

Tool results are also untrusted. A web page, email, document, issue, or database
field can contain an indirect prompt injection. InjecAgent and AgentDojo show
that poisoned external content can induce harmful calls or data disclosure in
tool-using agents [@zhan2024injecagent; @debenedetti2024agentdojo]. Returned prose
cannot grant authority, alter policy, approve a pending action, or widen the tool
catalog. The runtime handles it as tainted data with source provenance.

### Bind approval to what will execute

A human approves the **exact effect**, the normalized call that will execute,
rather than the model's description of it. The approval view shows the tool,
normalized arguments, target resource, current resource version, principal,
tenant, data leaving the boundary, expected postcondition, and rollback or
irreversibility. The approval record includes a digest of that
payload, the approver, the policy version, and an expiry.

Immediately before execution, trusted code rechecks authority and resource
state. If the arguments, resource, principal, policy version, or relevant state
has changed, the approval expires and the runtime must re-authorize or ask
again. An approval covers one execution of one payload; it is never a reusable
bearer capability and never enters model context as a secret token.

## Use MCP as a wire protocol

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool discovery and invocation,
schemas, transports, protocol metadata, and optional HTTP authorization. The
final `2026-07-28` revision uses a stateless protocol core: request metadata
carries the protocol revision and capabilities, while stateful tools expose
explicit application handles [@mcp2026release; @mcp2026tools].

Interoperability at the wire level still requires a client and server with
compatible revisions, transports, content types, authorization flows, and
extensions, so version negotiation and capability negotiation are tested for
the exact pair being deployed. Conformance to the wire format does not grant
trust, business authorization, safe retry semantics, data rights, or permission
to expose a newly discovered tool.

Five specific limits follow:

- `inputSchema` and `outputSchema` validate data shape; they do not establish a
  precondition, postcondition, side-effect class, or authority.
- A JSON-RPC request ID correlates protocol messages; it is not a business
  idempotency key.
- A state handle names state and carries no authority, so the server rechecks
  its owner and tenant on every call.
- Tool discovery returns an inventory, and a listed tool carries no endorsement.
  The deployment pins server identity, package digest, schema digest, and
  reviewed catalog, and quarantines unexpected catalog changes.
- A gateway can centralize routing, metering, and policy; authorization still
  happens at the MCP server and at the external resource.

HTTP authorization is optional in MCP. Where it is used, the client and server
must validate issuer, signature, expiry, token audience, and intended resource.
The authorization specification prohibits **token passthrough**: a server cannot
accept a token meant for another service and relay it downstream
[@mcp2026authorization]. The client-to-MCP credential stays separate from any
server-to-downstream credential. Otherwise a proxy with ambient authority,
credentials it holds and applies to every request, can become a **confused
deputy**, a privileged component that a caller tricks into using that authority
on the caller's behalf; per-client consent, audience binding, minimal scopes,
and independent resource authorization are required [@mcp2026security].

Local stdio servers are subprocesses with the host authority they inherit. Only
pinned and reviewed binaries run as local servers, under an unprivileged
identity, with explicit filesystem, environment, process, and network
restrictions. Calling the subprocess through MCP does not sandbox it.

## Specify the sandbox from a threat model

A @gls-sandbox is an execution boundary for code and processes whose behavior
cannot be trusted. It reduces the consequences of a compromised model, poisoned
tool output, malicious dependency, or ordinary bug. Whether an action is
authorized, and whether data may be disclosed, are decided outside it.

Sandbox design starts from a **threat model**, which names the attacker and the
protected assets:

- host escape or access to another tenant;
- cross-tenant or cross-run data disclosure;
- data exfiltration through network, logs, artifacts, or allowed services;
- denial of service through CPU, memory, process, disk, output, or network use;
- supply chain execution from packages, images, extensions, and build scripts;
- unwanted persistence in overlays, snapshots, caches, logs, or external APIs;
- theft or replay of credentials; and
- abuse by a trusted operator or compromised control plane.

Isolation is a conjunction of separate guarantees:

$$
G = K \land P \land F \land N \land I \land R \land T \land C,
$$

where $G$ is the claimed sandbox guarantee; $K$ is the kernel or system-call
boundary; $P$ is process, user, IPC, and tenant isolation; $F$ is filesystem,
mount, device, and artifact isolation; $N$ is ingress and network egress policy;
$I$ is workload identity and credential authority; $R$ is resource control;
$T$ is workspace lifetime, persistence, cleanup, and data-remanence control; and
$C$ is control-plane integrity, patching, audit, and configuration. If any term
needed by the threat model is absent, the overall claim does not hold.

### Compare mechanisms by call path

| Mechanism | Boundary introduced | Important limits |
|---|---|---|
| Hardened container | Linux namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, seccomp, and an LSM constrain a process on a shared host kernel | Correct configuration and host patching remain critical; application syscalls reach the shared kernel implementation |
| Userspace kernel | A Sentry-like layer reimplements much of the guest ABI and makes a restricted set of host calls | The userspace kernel, file broker, host kernel, and control plane remain trusted; compatibility and cost are workload-specific |
| MicroVM | A guest kernel and virtual device model run across a VMM and hardware virtualization boundary | The VMM, KVM, host kernel, jailer, storage, networking, snapshot path, and control plane remain trusted |
| Language isolate | V8, WebAssembly, or another runtime exposes a deliberately small host API | Appropriate only when the task fits that API; host bindings and runtime implementation are the boundary |
| Browser process | Renderer sandbox and site isolation separate hostile web content from privileged browser components | Browser control still reaches accounts, cookies, downloads, local endpoints, and real external effects |

Firecracker demonstrates how a small virtual machine monitor can combine a
separate guest kernel with a reduced device model for serverless workloads
[@agache2020firecracker]. gVisor inserts a userspace application kernel rather
than passing application syscalls directly to the host, but its Sentry and host
interfaces are still part of the trusted surface [@gvisor2026security]. NIST's
container guidance likewise treats images, registries, orchestrators, runtimes,
hosts, and data as separate risk areas [@nist2017containers].

A microVM, userspace kernel, hardened container, language isolate, or browser
executor may each be the appropriate choice under a particular threat model.
Deployments layer mechanisms so that the failure of one boundary is contained
by another, and test the configured system. Startup time, density,
compatibility, accelerators, snapshot support, and cost are workload
measurements and establish nothing about isolation.

### Define the complete sandbox envelope

An isolation label leaves most operational authority unspecified. A deployable
sandbox envelope, the full set of limits the runtime enforces around one run,
pins the enforcement points:

```yaml
sandbox:
  image_digest: sha256:<immutable-image>
  runtime_revision: <runtime-and-host-policy-version>
  identity: {tenant: acme, run_id: run_85a, uid: 10000}
  filesystem:
    root: read_only
    inputs: [{digest: sha256:<input>, mode: read_only}]
    workspace: {mode: fresh_overlay, max_bytes: 2147483648}
    devices: []
  network_egress:
    default: deny
    allowed_destinations: [artifact-mirror.internal]
    methods: [GET]
    max_bytes: 104857600
  resources:
    cpu: 2
    memory_bytes: 4294967296
    process_count: 128
    disk_bytes: 2147483648
    open_files: 512
    output_bytes: 16777216
    wall_clock: 10m
  workspace_lifetime: one_run
  artifacts: {allow: [result.json], scan: true, hash: true}
  cleanup: {lease: 15m, revoke_credentials: true, verify_process_tree: true}
```

The runtime enforces the filesystem mounts, read-only inputs, network egress,
CPU, memory, process count, disk, file descriptor, output, and wall-clock limits
outside the workload. Limits cover descendants, not only the first process.
Allowed network destinations are resolved and revalidated through trusted DNS;
IPv4, IPv6, redirects, alternate protocols, and metadata endpoints receive the
same policy.

### Keep credentials outside the workload

The invariant is that untrusted execution receives no reusable ambient
authority; trusted components outside the workload may still hold credentials.
The preferred design is a semantic action broker outside the sandbox, a service
that performs named operations on the workload's behalf so that the workload
never holds the credential. Where direct model access is necessary, the workload
receives a @gls-virtual-key issued by a @gls-gateway, a short-lived scoped
substitute for a provider key. No raw provider key enters the sandbox.

Other services issue a **short-lived token** bound to workload identity,
tenant, audience, resource, action, and expiry. Where a service cannot issue one,
**egress substitution** may exchange a placeholder at a trusted proxy, but the
proxy must bind the request to the exact allowed destination, method, path,
quota, and operation. Otherwise the proxy becomes a credentialed confused
deputy. Credentials stay out of images, workspace snapshots, exported artifacts,
crash dumps, model context, and logs, and are revoked when the lease ends.

A default-deny network policy still leaves paths that tests must cover: DNS
rebinding, redirects, raw IP addresses, IPv6, WebSockets, uploads to an allowed
host, and cloud metadata endpoints. Permission to reach a hostname does not
extend to every action on that host.

### Treat workspace state as a governed artifact

Every ephemeral run starts from a **clean baseline**, an immutable image digest
plus explicit read-only inputs. The run record holds the input digest,
dependency locks, tool versions, runtime and kernel revisions, locale, clock and
randomness policy, resource limits, and network fixtures. A **workspace
snapshot** is mutable state, not a clean baseline; it can retain processes,
credentials, randomness state, caches, and malicious files.

Only declared paths are exported. Outputs are scanned for malware, secrets,
unexpected repositories, links, device files, archives, and executable content,
and each output digest and its artifact provenance are recorded before the
controller consumes or publishes the artifact. Failed or suspicious outputs
enter quarantine. A reset test proves that
a fresh run cannot read a canary written by the prior run, including through
snapshots, caches, backing volumes, logs, or exported images.

Persistent workspaces are a separate feature with a separate retention and
authorization policy. Suspending a process does not make its state safe or
reproducible. Deleting an overlay also does not erase external API effects,
backups, or retained logs.

### Give browser agents two boundaries

A browser agent needs both web-content isolation and tenant isolation. A fresh
browser profile separates cookies and storage for the run. The renderer sandbox
and site isolation constrain hostile pages. An outer microVM, userspace kernel,
or hardened container protects the broker and other tenants. A separate action
policy governs navigation, downloads, uploads, clipboard, file URLs, local and
metadata addresses, authenticated writes, and payments.

WebDriver is a privileged remote-control interface [@w3c2026webdriver], so it
stays off the sandbox network, and a run never reuses a personal browser
profile. A browser sandbox can contain renderer code while the automated browser
still misuses a legitimate account.

### Coding agents as a deployed system

Coding agents are the filesystem harness from the control-pattern table,
deployed as products at a scale that vendors, researchers, and independent
evaluators have documented: vendors publish usage figures, production traces
have been characterized, and evaluators have measured the products. Claude
Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot's cloud agent take a task in natural
language, check out a repository, edit files, run shell commands, install
dependencies, run the project's tests and linters, and return a diff, a branch,
or a pull request. A hosted Codex task, for example, creates a container, checks
out the repository at the selected branch or commit, runs a setup script, and
reads the project's lint and test commands from an `AGENTS.md` file
[@openai2026codexenvironments]. Claude Code and Codex also run locally under
the developer's account, where the sandbox is built from operating-system
primitives.

The workload executes code by design. Test suites, build scripts, package
install hooks, and Git hooks are programs from the repository and its
dependencies, and the task input, such as an issue, a README, or a fetched page,
can carry an indirect prompt injection. Every item of the threat model above
therefore applies during an ordinary run.

Per-command approval does not scale to a task that runs many shell commands, so
these products approve a boundary instead. In its auto-allow mode, Claude Code's
sandbox runs a command without a prompt when the command stays inside the
declared paths and network domains. Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux
enforce the boundary for the command and its child processes, and a command
retried outside the sandbox goes back through the ordinary permission flow
[@anthropic2026claudecodesandbox]. Anthropic's account of the design requires
filesystem and network isolation together: without the network half, a
compromised agent can send out files such as SSH keys; without the filesystem
half, it can escape the sandbox and gain network access
[@anthropic2025sandboxing].

The filesystem defaults show where the remaining gaps are. Claude Code makes the
working directory and a session temporary directory writable, but still denies
writes there to files that are loaded or executed later in another context,
such as `.git/hooks`, `.gitconfig`, shell startup files, and the agent's own
settings and hooks, because a command that edited them could grant itself
permissions or register code that runs outside the sandbox. Its default read
scope is the whole machine, so `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.ssh/` stay readable
until a credential rule denies them [@anthropic2026claudecodesandbox].

The network decision follows the phases of a task: dependency installation
needs a package registry, while editing and testing usually need no outside
host. Codex runs the setup script with internet access and blocks access in the
agent phase by default, with a domain allowlist and an option that permits only
GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests; its documentation gives prompt injection hidden
in an issue description as the reason [@openai2026codexinternet]. An allowlist
bounds destinations and leaves actions open. Claude Code's documentation warns
that allowing a broad domain such as `github.com` can open an exfiltration path,
and that its hostname-based proxy may be bypassed through domain fronting, where
a request's visible hostname differs from the host that serves it
[@anthropic2026claudecodesandbox].

Credentials follow from what the agent must deliver. Pushing a branch, fetching
private packages, and calling the model all need authority, in an environment
that runs the repository's own code. The products keep that authority outside
the workload or narrow it to one operation:

- Codex gives secrets to the setup script only and removes them before the
  agent phase starts [@openai2026codexenvironments].
- Claude Code on the web keeps git credentials and signing keys outside the
  sandbox behind a git proxy [@anthropic2025sandboxing]. Locally, a masked
  credential appears to sandboxed commands as a placeholder that the sandbox
  proxy replaces only on requests to declared hosts
  [@anthropic2026claudecodesandbox], which is the egress substitution described
  above.
- Copilot's cloud agent pushes only to one `copilot/` branch and cannot run Git
  commands itself. It cannot approve or merge its own pull request, the
  requesting user cannot approve it either, and workflows run on its changes
  only after a user with write access approves them [@github2026copilotrisks].

The workflow rule closes a path around the sandbox: a CI workflow can run with
repository secrets, so agent code that could trigger it unreviewed would regain
the authority that the sandbox withheld. Codex also caches container state for
up to 12 hours between tasks [@openai2026codexenvironments], which makes the
cached container a workspace snapshot in the sense above, mutable state with its
own retention and reset obligations.

Usage is published as several quantities, each with its own denominator and
measurer: revenue run-rate, active users of a product that also has features
without an agent, the share of a platform's pull requests that involve an
agent, survey self-reports, and production traces. None of them measures
accepted output or productivity. @sec-adoption-productivity separates adoption,
usage, capability, and realized value, and @sec-capability-horizon reviews the
controlled productivity studies.

Traces measure the load that agents place on serving. A characterization of
sampled GitHub Copilot traces by Microsoft researchers, not yet peer reviewed,
found that each user turn unfolds into an autonomous loop of model calls almost
always coupled with tool execution. Reuse of the key-value cache, the stored
attention state of a prompt prefix that spares the server from recomputing it,
is high within a turn and drops at turn boundaries, after model switches, and
after context compaction, which replaces older history with a summary
[@liu2026copilottraces]. @sec-memory-scheduling explains the prefix caching
involved. Capability measurements treat the product scaffold as part of the
system under test, as @sec-evaluating-agents requires, and METR has measured
time horizons, the task length in human working time that an agent completes at
a stated success rate, with Claude Code and Codex as the scaffold, METR's term
for the harness around the model [@metr2026scaffolds].

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

- Anthropic reported on 12 February 2026 that Claude Code's run-rate revenue
  exceeded USD 2.5 billion and that its weekly active users had doubled since
  1 January [@anthropic2026seriesg]. Both are company figures.
- Microsoft reported on 29 July 2026 that GitHub Copilot had 50 million users
  and that one in three pull requests on GitHub involved an agent
  [@microsoft2026fy26q4]. The user count covers the whole Copilot product, and
  the call did not define what involving an agent means.
- In Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, 14.1 percent of the 31,877
  respondents to the question used AI agents at work daily, 9 percent weekly,
  and 37.9 percent did not plan to [@stackoverflow2025ai]. The question covers
  AI agents in general.
- The June 2026 Copilot trace sample covers 3.2 million users, 13 million
  sessions, 761 million model calls, and 95 trillion tokens; key-value cache hit
  rates average 90 percent within a turn and 55 percent across turn boundaries
  [@liu2026copilottraces].
- METR reported on 13 February 2026 that neither Claude Code nor Codex
  outperformed its default scaffolds when measuring the time horizons of Claude
  Opus 4.5 and GPT-5. Claude Code beat METR's ReAct scaffold in 50.7 percent of
  bootstrap samples, and Codex beat its Triframe scaffold in 14.5 percent
  [@metr2026scaffolds].
:::

## Wire the runtime through separate enforcement points

The controller consumes services, and model, tool, state, and compute access
each cross their own enforcement point, so no single component holds all the
trust.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-agent-runtime
//| fig-cap: "An agent runtime with separate enforcement points. Durable control state stays separate from model serving, tool authorization, and sandbox supervision; each external effect passes an independently enforced check."
digraph runtime {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  app [label="User / application"];
  control [label="Trusted controller\ncontract • policy • budget"];
  seams [shape=record, label="{Model gateway\nscoped access • usage|Tool policy + broker\nauth • approval • credentials|Sandbox supervisor\nimage • limits • cleanup|Durable event log\ncheckpoint • receipts}"];
  evidence [label="External evidence\ntraces • artifacts • outcomes"];

  app -> control;
  control -> seams [label="separate\nenforcement"];
  seams -> evidence [label="decisions +\nreceipts"];
}
```

The model gateway in @sec-serving-stack and @sec-wiring-stack controls model
identity, routing, budget, and usage. The tool broker authenticates the caller,
authorizes the exact effect, and obtains narrowly scoped credentials. The
sandbox supervisor allocates the boundary, applies resource and egress policy,
and reconciles cleanup. Durable state records decisions and receipts. No single
gateway log is sufficient evidence for all four paths.

## Record evidence that supports recovery and audit

An observability trace helps diagnose a run; an audit record supports an
accountability claim; an event log supports recovery. They may share identifiers
without becoming the same object.

The minimum record contains:

- run ID, attempt ID, trace ID, parent span, timestamps, and controller
  revision;
- user or workload principal, tenant, delegated actor, and authority expiry;
- model revision, prompt and context-builder versions, token use, and latency;
- tool version and schema digest, normalized argument digest, resource identity,
  policy decision, policy version, and denial reason;
- approval identity, exact approved payload digest, expiry, and revalidation;
- idempotency key, retry number, effect receipt, external state version, and
  compensation;
- sandbox image digest, runtime policy, resource usage, network destinations,
  artifact digests, and cleanup evidence; and
- terminal reason, success evidence, unresolved ambiguity, and last-known-good
  release.

W3C Trace Context standardizes how a trace ID and parent span propagate across
services; it does not define agent semantics or guarantee that every relevant
event was sampled and retained [@w3c2021trace]. Tokens, reusable credentials,
and sensitive payloads stay out of logs by default. The event sink sits outside
the sandbox under retention and access policy, and tests confirm that crashes
and denied actions still leave a complete record.

## Verify failure behavior before granting authority

Evaluation covers the final answer, external end state, policy compliance,
trajectory, latency, cost, and repeated-run reliability. @sec-eval-practice
provides the statistical harness. Agent-specific acceptance tests also exercise
the control plane:

| Scenario | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Indirect prompt injection or malicious tool output | No authority gain, no policy rewrite, taint and provenance retained |
| Malformed or drifting tool schema | Call rejected or catalog quarantined before model exposure |
| Wrong tenant, expired token, wrong audience, or token passthrough | Denied independently at broker and resource; no downstream effect |
| Stale approval or changed arguments | Approval invalidated; fresh exact-effect decision required |
| Duplicate delivery or retry after ambiguous write | One logical effect or explicit reconciliation and escalation |
| Worker crash before and after the external effect | Resume from event log without silent loss or repetition |
| Timeout or cancellation during a tool | Descendants stopped, late result quarantined, terminal reason recorded |
| Fork bomb, memory pressure, disk fill, or output flood | CPU, memory, process, disk, and output limits contain the run |
| Filesystem escape or peer-canary read | Access denied; host and cross-tenant canaries remain unreadable |
| Egress attempt by raw IP, redirect, IPv6, or allowed-host upload | External default-deny policy blocks the undeclared action |
| Browser navigation to local services or destructive authenticated action | Origin and action policy blocks or requests fresh approval |
| Cleanup-controller failure | Lease reconciliation removes processes, storage, credentials, and billable resources |

These tests run through the deployed model gateway, tool server, policy engine,
sandbox image, and controller rather than through mocks of the boundary under
test. A high-impact write goes first through shadow execution, which runs the
new release on live inputs without letting its effects through, or through a
simulator, then to a canary tenant with a narrow failure budget. The
last-known-good route stays live until the canary satisfies both task and
containment gates.

## Operate the agent lifecycle

A practical sequence is:

1. **Freeze the contract.** Define task boundary, success evidence, permitted
   effects, authority, data, budgets, terminal reasons, recovery, and rollback.
2. **Build the smallest explicit loop.** Keep deterministic work in code and use
   the model only where the contract requires uncertain interpretation or choice.
3. **Specify every tool.** Pin schemas and implementation digests; add policy,
   idempotency, errors, data, credentials, and postconditions.
4. **Choose control semantics.** Select linear loop, state graph, durable
   workflow, filesystem harness, or supervisor and worker from the transitions
   the task needs.
5. **Choose and test isolation.** Start from the threat model, define the full
   sandbox envelope, and run escape, exfiltration, resource, remanence, and
   cleanup tests.
6. **Rehearse recovery.** Use failure injection for worker crashes, duplicate
   callbacks, timeouts, cancellation, stale approval, and ambiguous external
   outcomes.
7. **Seal the release.** Bind model, prompt, controller, tool catalog, policy,
   sandbox image, state schema, and evaluation plan to digests.
8. **Evaluate and shadow.** Measure success, external state, policy compliance,
   repeated-run reliability, cost, latency, and failure containment.
9. **Canary with narrow authority.** Use limited tenants, tools, credentials,
   egress, concurrency, and spend while the last-known-good route remains live.
10. **Monitor and requalify.** Review failures, reconcile leases and ambiguous
    effects, rotate credentials, patch boundaries, and rerun affected gates.

A **requalification trigger** includes a model revision, prompt or context change,
controller or state migration, tool schema or implementation change, policy
change, authorization flow, sandbox image or runtime change, new host or device,
browser revision, network policy, artifact pipeline, tenant boundary, or material
traffic shift. Each trigger creates a new release identity and reruns the tests
for the affected enforcement boundaries.

The output is an agent release record linking the agent execution contract,
controller and state schema, model revision, tool and policy digests, sandbox
envelope, approval and effect evidence, evaluation report, canary result, and
rollback outcome. Operating, auditing, and rolling back the agent all start from
that record; the framework name identifies only one of its components.

## Lower-layer constraint

The controller cannot recover an effect that the external API cannot identify,
contain code outside the boundary enforced by the host, or reconstruct evidence
that the gateways and event store never recorded. Model serving limits shape
latency and cost; tool and identity systems shape authority; storage shapes
recovery; compute and network policy shape containment. The agent contract must
fit those lower-layer guarantees.

Conversely, a microVM or durable workflow cannot rescue an overbroad business
permission. Isolation limits where code runs. Authorization limits what the
verified principal may do. Both must hold at the execution boundary described in
@sec-security-authorization.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

There is no settled best framework, orchestration pattern, or isolation
mechanism for every agent. More model autonomy can reduce controller code while
making trajectories harder to bound. More explicit workflow structure can
improve recovery while increasing state and migration work. A separate guest
kernel, a userspace kernel, a hardened shared kernel, and a language runtime
present different trusted surfaces rather than one permanent ranking.

The reversible decision is to grant the smallest measured authority, expose the
smallest tool set, preserve a deterministic policy boundary, and require the
candidate to pass both task and containment tests. Product choice can then
change without changing the execution contract.
:::

## Further reading

The primary papers establish the action pattern and observed attack surface;
the standards and systems sources define tool, authorization, tracing, durable
execution, and isolation boundaries.
